architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added Envoy Gateway as an optional Helm subchart dependency with two deployment modes (bundled-controller and external-controller)
architecture_decisions.rationale: This approach provides flexibility for different deployment scenarios. Self-hosted/single-tenant clusters can use the bundled controller, while shared clusters with existing platform controllers can use external-controller mode. Using the official envoyproxy/gateway-helm chart ensures compatibility and reduces maintenance burden.
alternatives_considered: Building custom Envoy Gateway manifests from scratch
Using a different API gateway solution like Kong or Traefik

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added a dedicated Redis/Sentinel deployment specifically for Envoy global rate limiting, separate from the existing app Redis
architecture_decisions.rationale: Rate limiting requires high availability and persistence to maintain state across Envoy instances. A separate Redis instance prevents rate limiting operations from interfering with application caching and ensures isolation of concerns. The Sentinel configuration provides HA failover capabilities.
alternatives_considered: Sharing the existing app Redis instance
Using an in-memory rate limiting solution without persistence

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Implemented granular rate limiting policies for different API routes with configurable thresholds
architecture_decisions.rationale: Different API endpoints have different usage patterns and security requirements. For example, authentication endpoints need stricter limits than client API endpoints. The implementation uses BackendTrafficPolicy resources with distinct rules for IPv4 and IPv6 traffic, and includes header-based rate limiting for management APIs using x-api-key.
alternatives_considered: Global rate limiting for all endpoints
Application-level rate limiting instead of gateway-level

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added comprehensive validation templates to prevent misconfiguration
architecture_decisions.rationale: Envoy Gateway configuration is complex with many interdependent options. The validation template ensures users get clear error messages when they enable features without required dependencies (e.g., enabling controller without Redis, or enabling ingress without host configuration). This prevents runtime failures and improves user experience.

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Used helper functions to generate consistent resource names and handle defaults
architecture_decisions.rationale: Kubernetes resource names have length constraints (63 characters) and naming conventions. The helper functions in _helpers.tpl ensure generated names are truncated properly and follow consistent patterns. They also provide sensible defaults while allowing overrides for advanced users.
alternatives_considered: Requiring users to specify all resource names

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Created separate ingress resource for Envoy API traffic with explicit host validation
architecture_decisions.rationale: When both the main app ingress and Envoy API ingress are enabled, they need different hosts to avoid routing conflicts. The implementation requires explicit host configuration in this scenario and provides clear error messages. The ingress supports all Formbricks API routes (auth, client v1/v2, management, webhooks, storage) with configurable path routing.
alternatives_considered: Using the same ingress as the main app
Requiring manual ingress configuration outside the chart

implementation_summary:
The implementation adds an optional Envoy Gateway bundle to the Formbricks Helm chart, providing API gateway capabilities with sophisticated rate limiting. The approach is opt-in by default, with all Envoy components disabled unless explicitly enabled through configuration values.

Key patterns used include: 1) Flexible deployment modes supporting both bundled-controller (for self-hosted clusters) and external-controller (for shared clusters with existing controllers); 2) Separation of concerns with a dedicated Redis/Sentinel deployment specifically for Envoy rate limiting, distinct from the application Redis; 3) Granular, configurable rate limiting policies that can be enabled separately from the initial deployment; and 4) Comprehensive validation to prevent misconfiguration.

The changes integrate cleanly with the existing codebase by extending the Helm chart's dependency management system, adding new template files that conditionally render based on configuration values, and maintaining backward compatibility. The implementation follows Kubernetes Gateway API standards and uses the official Envoy Gateway Helm chart as a subchart dependency, ensuring compatibility with upstream releases. All resource naming follows consistent patterns using helper functions, and the configuration provides sensible defaults while allowing extensive customization for advanced use cases.
